title: Bubble sort
summary: Your first sorting algorithm: swap neighbours until nothing moves.

cards.title: Why sort at all?
cards.body:
Games sort constantly: leaderboards by score, sprites by depth so far things draw first, loot by rarity.

Sorted data is also **searchable** fast (binary search needs it). Sorting is the gateway skill.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body:
Walk along the list and compare each pair of **neighbours**. If the left one is bigger, swap them.

After one full walk (a **pass**), the biggest value has "bubbled" all the way to the end. Repeat for the rest.
Yellow = being compared. Purple = just swapped. Green = in its final place.

cards.title: The code
cards.body:
Two loops: the outer one counts passes, the inner one walks the unsorted part. `rec` only records pictures for the app, so ignore it.

The `swapped` flag is a free speed-up: if a pass swaps nothing, the list is already sorted, so we stop.

cards.title: How fast is it?
cards.body:
With n values, the first pass makes n-1 comparisons, the next n-2, and so on. In total that's about **n²/2** comparisons.

So bubble sort is **O(n²)**. Double the input and you get roughly 4x the work. For 1,000,000 items that is far too slow. Bubble sort is for learning, not for shipping.

cards.question: After the **first** pass of bubble sort on `[4, 2, 7, 1]`, which value is guaranteed to be in its final position?
cards.explain: Each pass carries the largest unsorted value to the end. 7 is the largest, so it ends at the last position.

cards.question: What does the `swapped` flag buy us on an already sorted list of n items?
cards.explain: The first pass makes no swaps, so the loop breaks. One pass of n-1 comparisons is O(n), the best case.
